planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; Brother Stefan is a giant-class hosta needing significant room to reach full size over several seasons.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, allowing generous room since this is a giant-class hosta that takes several years to reach its full mature spread. Brother Stefan bears huge, heavily corrugated, bright chartreuse-gold leaves that brighten a shaded bed and hold their color well into summer before mellowing slightly, with pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer providing a secondary, minor season of interest. Its large scale makes it an effective anchor or focal specimen in a woodland or shade border, best given room to spread without crowding from smaller companions. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, watch for slug damage on the tender new growth in spring, and expect the plant to need several growing seasons before it reaches its full impressive size.

common_name: Victory Hosta (Large Green Hosta with Creamy-White Margin)

planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; Victory is a large, vigorous hosta needing ample room to display its full, imposing mature form.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving the plant ample room to reach its large mature size over several seasons. Victory bears substantial, deeply veined, deep green leaves edged in a wide, creamy-white to yellow margin, forming an imposing, symmetrical mound that makes a strong specimen or focal point in a shaded border, with pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in mid to late summer. Its large scale and clean variegation hold up well through the growing season without excessive fading. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, watch for slug damage on tender spring growth, and divide only when the clump becomes overly congested after many years, since large hostas resent frequent disturbance.

common_name: Olive Bailey Langdon Hosta (Blue-Green Hosta with Wide Gold Margin)

planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; the gold margin on Olive Bailey Langdon develops best with some morning sun.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, with some gentle morning sun helping to develop the fullest gold margin color. Olive Bailey Langdon bears large, heavily corrugated, blue-green leaves edged in a broad, bright gold-yellow margin, a bold two-tone combination that holds up well through the season and stands out strongly against plain green shade companions, with pale lavender flowers on tall scapes in summer. Its substantial size and strong variegation make it a good specimen plant in a mixed shade border. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, watch for slug damage on the tender new growth in spring, and divide congested clumps only after several years, since hostas generally resent frequent disturbance.

common_name: Invincible Hosta (Fragrant Glossy Green Vigorous Hosta)

planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; Invincible is noted for exceptional vigor, slug resistance, and fragrant flowers relative to most hosta cultivars.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously. Invincible forms a dense, glossy, deep green mound noted for exceptional vigor and unusually good resistance to slug damage compared with most hosta cultivars, quickly forming a full, healthy clump. It produces abundant, sweetly fragrant, near-white flowers in mid to late summer, a stronger scent than typical hosta flowers, which are usually a secondary feature; here the fragrance adds real value to a shaded seating area or path edge planted nearby. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous, healthy growth.

planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring or early fall, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil; Spilt Milk is grown for its unusual white speckled and streaked leaf pattern rather than a solid-color margin.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, setting the crown at the same depth it grew previously. Spilt Milk carries an unusual, irregular pattern of white speckles and streaks scattered across its green leaves, as though milk had literally been splashed and dried across the foliage, a distinctive break from the more common solid-margin or two-tone variegation patterns found in most hosta cultivars. The speckling is most pronounced on new growth in cooler spring conditions and may soften somewhat as summer heat sets in. Pale lavender flowers appear on scapes above the foliage in summer, though the unusual leaf pattern is the main ornamental draw. Mulch to conserve moisture and keep the shallow root system cool, watch for slug damage on tender new growth, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.
